- When sentiment is consistently negative or near-zero, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to recent highs.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct; cap forecast at +3% above peak or use 10-day moving average for stabilization.
- If sentiment shows strong bullish momentum (e.g., >0.67 for 3+ consecutive days), model tends to overreact; apply downward bias of 1–3% to prevent overbought overcorrection.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.3–0.67), model often underestimates mean reversion; add 1–2% upward bias to account for lingering momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, model frequently fails to capture short-term volatility; use 7-day rolling average to smooth out noise before projecting.
- If recent history shows strong downward trend (e.g., 3 consecutive drops >2%), model often ignores support; add 1–3% upward buffer to prevent premature bottoming.
- Sentiment spikes (e.g., >0.8) correlate with model overestimating; apply 1–2% downward correction to avoid “sentiment-driven” overreach.
- Model tends to lag in correcting for sentiment shifts; if sentiment turns negative within 3 days, adjust forecast downward by 1–3% per day until sentiment stabilizes.
